questions.problem: Find the surface area of the portion of the cylinder $z=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}$ that is bounded by the constraints $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}},\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}})^{2}+(0)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{\frac{4}{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\cdot y\,{|}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=\frac{x}{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}x.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 1 \\ u & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\text{d}u \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =4(\frac{\pi }{6}-0) \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the surface area of the portion of the cone $z=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ that is bounded by the constraints $0\le x\le 1$ and $1\le y\le 2.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,0\le x\le 1,\,1\le y\le 2.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})^{2}+(\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+1}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot (1-0)\cdot (2-1) \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the plane $z=2x+3y$ that is bounded by the constraints $0\le x\le 1$ and $1\le y\le 3.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=2x+3y,\,0\le x\le 1,\,1\le y\le 3.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+3y)=2, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+3y)=3,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2)^{2}+(3)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4+9}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{14}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{14}{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{14}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{14}\cdot (1-0)\cdot (3-1) \\  & =2\sqrt{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z={x}^{2}+2{y}^{2},\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})=2x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})=4y,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2x)^{2}+(4y)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}}.$

questions.problem: Find the surface area of the portion of the surface $z=3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\sqrt{2}y$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\sqrt{2}y,\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \operatorname{sin}⁡2x},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/f6200343142274ee2f5b3934cbe014ee24edf8177f3a544c38dc070bb7df83ef.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\sqrt{2}y)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\sqrt{2}y)=2\sqrt{2},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{2}+(2\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+9{cos}^{2}⁡x+8}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{9(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x)}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot y\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+{cos}^{2}⁡x,$ we get $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,\text{d}x.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & \frac{\pi }{2} \\ u & 2 & 1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{2}^{1}\sqrt{u}(-\text{d}u) \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2({2}^{3/2}-1) \\  & =4\sqrt{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the part of the surface $y=\frac{1}{xz}$ that lies inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}=2.$ From left to right, what are the missing expressions?
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $y=f(x,z)$ with $(x,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
y=\frac{1}{xz},\,{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 2.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂y}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{xz})=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}z}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{1}{xz})=-\frac{1}{x{z}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}z})}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{x{z}^{2}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{x}^{4}{z}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}{z}^{4}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}{{x}^{4}{z}^{4}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is

where 

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+({e}^{y})^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{2y}}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\cdot z\,{|}_{z=0}^{z={e}^{2y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\cdot {e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & 0 & 1/2 \\ u & 3 & e+2\end{aligned}
$$

$$

\begin{aligned}\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r & =-\pi {\int }_{4}^{3}\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\pi {\int }_{3}^{4}{u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\pi \cdot 2{({u}^{1/2})}_{3}^{4} \\  & =2\pi \cdot ({4}^{1/2}-{3}^{1/2}) \\  & =2\pi (2-\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the paraboloid $x=5+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ that is subject to the constraint ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 3.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x=5+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2},\,(y,z)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 3},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/66b05919a7644818eea7265ff3ae8fc3ced4ac7d1d6d30352f612649393c876a.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})=2y, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(5+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})=2z,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2y)^{2}+(2z)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le \sqrt{3},\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+4{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=8r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & \sqrt{3} \\ u & 1 & 13\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{13}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{13}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{13} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{13} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}[(13)^{3/2}-1] \\  & =\frac{\pi (13\sqrt{13}-1)}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the plane $z = y - 4x$ that is bounded by the constraints $0 \leq x \leq 2$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z = f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z = y - 4x, \qquad 0 \leq x \leq 2, \quad 0 \leq y \leq 1.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-4x)=-4, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-4x)=1,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-4)^{2}+(1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+16+1}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{18}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =3\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\cdot (2-0)\cdot (1-0) \\  & =6\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial y}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial z}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x = y+\sqrt 2 z, \qquad (y,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D = \big\{ (y,z) \: : \: 1 \leq y \leq 2, \: 1 \leq z \leq 3\big\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/240ac546b0dd725e392dd0bd475b2ef00eebce2594be5921285e227137538c46.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y+\sqrt{2}z)=1, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(y+\sqrt{2}z)=\sqrt{2},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(1)}^{2}+{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{4}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =2\cdot (2-1)\cdot (3-1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the cone $z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ that is subject to the constraints  $x^2 + y^2 \leq 4,\, x\geq 0$ and $y\geq 0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}, \qquad (x,y)\in D,
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x^2+y^2\leq 4, \, x\geq 0, \, y\geq 0 \big\},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/be8246dc3bfe1bf16af5d9913fc4e6aef58ddad282646a00d3e31120f6bf31e8.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})}^{2}+{(\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}r\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}r\,\text{d}r \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot [\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /2}\cdot {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =\pi \sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
